docs.text: VV4ML Documentation VV4ML is a Python library designed to streamline the verification and validation (V&V) process for machine learning models. Why VV4ML? VV4ML makes it as easy as possible to implement advanced techniques to ensure a specific ML model is verified, robust, and credible. Its primary aim is to provide excellent accessibility and straightforward implementation for users who want to build trustworthy AI systems without needing to be experts in formal verification. Whether you are testing for fairness, evaluating robustness against unexpected inputs, or validating model performance across different data slices, VV4ML provides the tools you need through a clean and intuitive API. Key Features Ease of Use: An intuitive Python API designed specifically for data scientists and ML engineers. Comprehensive V&V Tools: Ready-to-use modules for assessing model credibility, robustness, and fairness. Seamless Integration: Designed to work smoothly with your existing Machine Learning pipelines. Where to go from here? Check out the Installation Guide to get VV4ML set up on your machine. Read the Quickstart to see VV4ML in action in less than 5 minutes. Explore the User Guide for an in-depth look at advanced verification techniques.

docs.text: Configuration Guide VV4ML uses a declarative, configuration-driven approach. Instead of hardcoding paths, thresholds, and model parameters in your scripts, you can define your entire Machine Learning V&V pipeline in a single structured YAML file . Before execution, VV4ML validates this file using Pydantic to ensure type safety and prevent runtime failures deep into your pipeline. Complete YAML Template Here is a comprehensive blueprint of a vv4ml compliant config.yaml file containing all available blocks. # ============================================================================= # 1. Dataset Configuration # ============================================================================= dataset: name: "housing_model_v1" path: "data/raw/housing.csv" source: "internal_database" provenance: "data_engineering_team" version: "1.0.0" file_format: "csv" duplicate_rows: false format_metadata: delimiter: ";" decimal_separator: "." header_lines: 1 encoding: "UTF-8" inputs: - name: "feat_A" data_type: "float" # Options: float, int range: [-3.5, 3.5] # Automatically converted to tuple units: "scaled_score" missing_values_allowed: false outputs: - name: "target" data_type: "float" range: [0.0, 500.0] units: "k_euros" # ============================================================================= # 2. Gate Thresholds # ============================================================================= gate_thresholds: validation: - field: "target" metric: "RMSE" # See supported metrics below value: 15.0 verification: convergence: - field: "loss" metric: "StandardDeviation" value: 0.01 smoothness: - field: "target" metric: "MaximumRelativeErrorRatio" value: 0.5 numerical_error: - field: "target" metric: "MaxStandardDeviation" value: 1e-6 # ============================================================================= # 3. Test Configurations # ============================================================================= test_configurations: verification: convergence: n_rows: [500, 1000, 2500] existence: samples: 50 smoothness: sample_fraction: 0.5 perturbation_scaled_magnitude: 0.01 numerical_error: sets: 5 # ============================================================================= # 4. Model Development # ============================================================================= model_development: train_test_split: train_fraction: 0.8 method: "random" # Options: random, grouped preprocessing: normalization: false standardization: true optimization: optimization_method: "GridSearch" # Options: GridSearch, RandomizedSearchCV n_jobs: 1 cv: 5 scoring: None model_list: - type: "LinearRegressor" # Supported types listed below label: "baseline_linear" # Optional, defaults to type if omitted hyperparameters: {} - type: "RandomForestRegressor" optimization: feature_selection: null optimization_method: RandomizedSearchCV n_jobs: 1 cv: 5 hyperparameters: n_estimators: [50, 100, 150] max_depth: [5, 10, 150] min_samples_split: [2, 10] min_samples_leaf: [1, 4] Supported Reference Fields Metric Types When configuring gate_thresholds , the metric field strictly accepts one of the following exact strings: MaximumAbsoluteError , MeanRelativeError , MaximumRelativeErrorRatio StandardDeviation , MaxStandardDeviation RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error), PercentageRMSE Model types The model_list.type field supports the following algorithms out of the box: RandomForestRegressor XGBoostRegressor SupportVectorRegressor LinearRegressor MLPRegressor PLSRegression CatBoostRegressor GaussianProcessRegressor Python Usage Examples Loading a Valid Configuration To load your YAML configuration file in your Python workflow, use the built-in load_config utility. It handles path expansion (including ~ ) and triggers Pydantic validation. from vv4ml.config import load_config # Load and validate config = load_config("vv4ml_config.yaml") # Data is fully parsed print(f"Loaded pipeline: {config.dataset.name}") print(f"Train fraction: {config.model_development.train_test_split.train_fraction}") # Accessing the first configured smoothness threshold smoothness_gate = config.gate_thresholds.verification.smoothness[0] print(f"Gate metric: {smoothness_gate.metric} (Threshold: {smoothness_gate.value})") Validation Errors If you accidentally enter an invalid type (e.g. passing a string into a numeric threshold or an unsupported model type), Pydantic will raise a ValidationError . You can catch it with: from pydantic import ValidationError from vv4ml.config import load_config try: config = load_config("corrupted_config.yaml") except ValidationError as err: print("Configuration schema validation failed!") print(err.json(indent=2))

docs.text: Installation Requirements Before installing VV4ML, ensure your system meets the following requirements: Python >= 3.11 (Optional, but recommended) uv >= 0.11 Installing VV4ML You can install VV4ML using either pip or uv . We highly recommend using a virtual environment for your Python projects. Option 1: Using uv (Preferred) The preferred and fastest way to install VV4ML is via uv . If you are managing a project and want to add VV4ML as a dependency to your pyproject.toml , run: uv add vv4ml Alternatively, if you just want to install it into your active virtual environment, use: uv pip install vv4ml Option 2: Using pip (Standard) The standard way to install VV4ML is via pip . We recommend updating pip to the latest version before proceeding: pip install --upgrade pip Then install the library: pip install vv4ml

docs.text: Quickstart This guide walks you through a basic workflow: Preparing a model and dataset Running a Verification and Validation (V&V) checks Inspecting validation results Prerequisites To follow this quickstart, ensure you have VV4ML installed, along with scikit-learn and pandas to generate a simple test model: pip install vv4ml scikit-learn pandas Basic Smoothness Test Example A practical way to see VV4ML in action is by running a Smoothness Test . This test evaluates how stable your model's outputs are when subjected to small perturbations in the input features. Create a new Python file (e.g. smoothness_demo.py ) and paste the following example: import pandas as pd from sklearn.datasets import make_regression from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from vv4ml.verification.smoothness import run_smoothness_test # Prepare evaluation data as a pandas DataFrame X_raw, y_raw = make_regression(n_samples=2500, n_features=3, random_state=42) # Shift target values away from 0. scikit-learn's make_regression centers outputs around 0, # which causes numerical instability (division-by-zero effects) in the relative error metric. y_raw = y_raw + 1000 feature_names = ["feat_A", "feat_B", "feat_C"] x_eval = pd.DataFrame(X_raw, columns=feature_names) # Train a baseline model model = LinearRegression() model.fit(x_eval, y_raw) # Define the input ranges (min, max) for each dimension input_ranges = [(x_eval[col].min(), x_eval[col].max()) for col in x_eval.columns] # Run the test # In this example we sample 50% of the data, apply a 1% perturbation, and set an error ratio threshold 0f 0.5 result = run_smoothness_test( model=model, x_eval=x_eval, input_ranges=input_ranges, sample_fraction=0.5, perturbation_scaled_magnitude=0.01, threshold=0.5, random_state=42, ) # Inspect the verification results print(f"Test is passed: {result.passed}") print(f"Maximum Error Ration found: {result.max_error_ratio}") print(f"Threshold is set to {result.threshold}") Output When you run the script, VV4ML analyses the output and verify if they remain proportional and stable compared to the input perturbations. If so, test will pass. Let's roll these out: result.passed is True : your model behaviour is smooth within the defined threshold. result.passed is False : your model might exhibit sudden jumps or high sensitivity to specific feature changes Next Steps Learn how to drive your tests using YAML in the Configuration Guide . Explore other verification methods in the Verification module

docs.text: Convergence Test The Convergence module evaluates data volume convergence . It determines whether your model's performance has stabilized or if it would significantly benefit from more training data. By training the model on progressively larger subsets of your data, VV4ML analyses the stability of the resulting evaluation metrics. How It Works Mathematically Given a list of dataset sizes \([N_1, N_2, \dots, N_k]\) configured via YAML, VV4ML: 1. Subsamples the training dataset to match each specified \(n\) . 2. Trains the chosen model architecture on each subset. 3. Computes the target metric (e.g., RMSE or StandardDeviation ) for each step. 4. Checks if the metric stabilizes. If the metric fluctuation (measured via StandardDeviation ) across the largest data sizes is below your threshold, the test passes: \[ \sigma(\text{metrics}_{k-2}, \text{metrics}_{k-1}, \text{metrics}_k) \le \text{threshold} \] YAML Configuration To activate and configure this test, define the convergence blocks under both gate_thresholds and test_configurations : ```yaml gate_thresholds: verification: convergence: - field: "loss" metric: "StandardDeviation" # Checks the stability of the metric value: 0.01 # Maximum allowed standard deviation test_configurations: verification: convergence: n_rows: [500, 1000, 2500] # Subsets of data to evaluate
